entries.title: The politics of policy transfer: political dynamics in OECD accession
entries.abstract: While recent scholarship has called for greater attention to the political dynamics of policy transfer, this dimension remains under-theorised in policy studies. entries.title: Explaining policy stasis on same-sex unions in Peru
entries.abstract: This article advances understanding of how policy monopolies sustain policy stasis in morality policy, where scholarship has explained policy change more fully than its absence. It develops the concept of a moral policy monopoly to examine how interlocking mechanisms can sustain policy stasis in contexts of high religiosity. Using abductive, mechanistic and analyticist process tracing, and drawing on documents and interviews, the study examines three decades of legislative inertia on same-sex unions in Peru, where 17 Bills were submitted to Congress between 1993 and 2024 and none advanced to plenary approval. The analysis identifies five interlocking mechanisms through which ultraconservative religious actors sustain stasis under conditions of high religiosity, substantial church capacity and a religiously embedded party system. entries.title: Why policy actors choose not to coordinate in policy conflicts
entries.abstract: Research on advocacy coalitions in public policy highlights the importance of coordination among policy actors seeking to influence policy making. Less attention has been devoted to why actors sometimes choose not to coordinate, even when they share similar beliefs or interests. In this study, we explore the rationales behind actors’ decisions to refrain from publicly visible coordination in wind power development projects in two Swedish municipalities over a 16-year period. entries.title: Negotiating Competing Expectations—Chiefs and Mineral Governance in Ghana
entries.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines what shapes chiefs' discretionary decision‐making and how they exercise authority within hybrid governance arrangements, focusing on Ghana's artisanal and small‐scale mining (ASM) sector. Existing scholarship recognizes that traditional authorities can strengthen or undermine state governance but offers limited explanations for variation in their practices. Drawing on interviews with chiefs, miners, and state officials, the paper develops a discretionary governance framework that integrates hybrid governance, access theory, and discretion. It argues that overlapping customary and statutory authority creates a discretionary space for chiefs to navigate competing expectations.
